title: Present Value and Future Value
summary: Why a dollar today beats a dollar next year, and how to move money backwards and forwards through time.

lesson.body:
Offer almost anyone $1,000 today or $1,000 in three years and they take the money now. That instinct is the entire subject of [[time-value-of-money]]: a dollar has a date attached to it, and dollars with different dates are different things. You cannot add them, compare them, or average them until you have moved them to a common point in time.

Moving money forward in time gives you a [[future-value]]. Moving it backwards gives you a [[present-value]]. Every valuation you will ever see — a bond, a company, a fund's projected distributions — is some version of moving future money back to today and adding it up.

Why is today's dollar worth more? Three reasons stack up.

First, **opportunity**. A dollar in your hand can be put to work — in a deposit, a bond, a business. Waiting means giving that up, so you should be paid for waiting.

Second, **risk**. A promise of $1,000 in three years might not be kept. The less certain the promise, the more you demand for accepting it.

Third, and least interesting, **inflation**. If prices rise, the same nominal dollar buys less later.

The rate that captures all of this in one number is the [[discount-rate]]. And here is the part that surprises people: the effect is not linear. Interest earns interest, which earns interest — [[compounding]]. Over one year, compounding barely matters. Over twenty, it dominates everything else in the calculation.

lesson.plainReading: Future value equals today's amount, multiplied by one-plus-the-rate, raised to the number of periods. The exponent is where [[compounding]] lives: each period multiplies the whole balance again, not just the original amount.

variables.meaning: the amount at the end — the [[future-value]]
the rate per period, as a decimal (6% is 0.06)
the number of periods — not necessarily years

lesson.plainReading: Present value equals the future amount divided by one-plus-the-rate raised to the number of periods. It is simply the future-value formula rearranged — discounting and compounding are the same operation pointed in opposite directions.

variables.meaning: the [[discount-factor]] — the number you multiply a future dollar by to get today's value

lesson.body: Take $5,000 and a [[required-return]] of 6% a year, and run it in both directions.
walkthrough: **Forward, three years.** Multiply by 1.06 once per year: 1.06 x 1.06 x 1.06 = 1.191016. So FV = $5,000 x 1.191016 = **$5,955.08**.

Notice the total gain is $955.08, not $900. Simple interest at 6% on $5,000 would be $300 a year, or $900 over three years. The extra $55.08 is [[compounding]] — interest that the earlier interest earned.
**Backwards, three years.** Now ask what $5,000 received in three years is worth today. Divide instead of multiply: $5,000 / 1.191016 = **$4,198.10**.
The [[discount-factor]] here is 1 / 1.191016 = 0.8394. Every dollar arriving in three years is worth about 84 cents today at a 6% discount rate.

Sanity check the direction of both answers. Money moved *forward* got bigger; money moved *backwards* got smaller. If your answer goes the other way, you have divided when you meant to multiply — which is the single most common arithmetic slip in this topic.

lesson.body:
The hardest part of this topic is not the algebra, it is knowing what number to use for r. The [[discount-rate]] is not handed to you by nature; it is a judgement about what return you require for taking this particular risk over this particular horizon.

A government bond cash flow gets discounted at something close to a [[risk-free-rate]]. A late-stage venture company's projected exit gets discounted at something far higher, because the promise is far shakier. Same formula, wildly different r — and because r sits inside an exponent, small disagreements about it produce enormous disagreements about value.

lesson.caption: Discount factors: what one future dollar is worth today

lesson.body:
Read the bottom-right corner of that table and let it land: at a 12% discount rate, a dollar arriving in twenty years is worth about **ten cents** today.

This is why long-dated, uncertain cash flows are so hard to value and so easy to argue about. It is also why rising rates hurt long-duration assets most — the far-future cash flows, which carry the largest exponent, get crushed first. Read down any column to see time compounding against you; read across any row to see the rate doing the same thing.

**Your rate and your periods must speak the same language.** A 6% annual rate over 3 years means r = 0.06 and n = 3. If cash flows are quarterly, you need a quarterly rate and a quarterly count: r = 0.015 and n = 12, not r = 0.06 and n = 12.

Mixing them is the most common wrong answer on exam questions of this type, and it is a real error in spreadsheets too — a monthly model wired to an annual rate overstates value by a wide margin. Before you compute anything, say out loud what one period is.

You will meet this within your first month, usually without anyone calling it time value of money.

A private fund projects that it will return capital in years 6 through 9. To compare that against a fund returning capital in years 3 through 5, you cannot just add up the dollars — you discount them, and the earlier fund looks better than the raw totals suggest. This is the arithmetic underneath why the [[j-curve]] matters and why an [[internal-rate-of-return]] can flatter a fund that returned money early.

It also shows up whenever someone says a valuation is "rate sensitive". What they mean is that r sits in an exponent, so moving it a little moves the answer a lot.

items: Dollars carry dates. Move them to a common date before comparing, adding, or averaging.
Compounding and discounting are one operation in two directions: multiply by (1+r)^n going forward, divide by it coming back.
Because r sits in an exponent, value is far more sensitive to the discount rate the further out the cash flow is.
Match your rate to your period. Quarterly cash flows need a quarterly rate and a quarterly period count.

questions.stem: Ignoring inflation entirely, why would a rational investor still prefer $1,000 today over a guaranteed $1,000 in two years?
choices: Because the money today can be invested to earn a return over those two years
Because $1,000 in two years is not really $1,000
Because inflation is the only reason money loses value over time
Because two years is too long to wait for any investor
rationales: Correct. Even with zero inflation and zero default risk, holding the money now gives you the option to put it to work. Giving that up is a real cost, and the [[discount-rate]] is what compensates you for it.
The future payment genuinely is $1,000 in nominal terms. What differs is what it is worth *today*, which is a statement about discounting, not about the amount being misstated.

This inverts the lesson. Inflation is one of three reasons and the least fundamental — opportunity cost alone is enough to make today's dollar worth more, which is exactly what the question stipulates by ruling inflation out.
Investor patience is not the mechanism. Plenty of investors happily lock money up for twenty years — they simply demand to be paid for it.
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the load-bearing reason for the [[time-value-of-money]]. Risk and inflation add to the required rate, but even a perfectly safe, inflation-free world would still discount future cash flows.

questions.stem: You invest $5,000 today at 6% a year, compounded annually. What is it worth after 3 years?
questions.inputHint: Answer in dollars, to the nearest cent. Do not type a $ sign.
questions.explanation: FV = 5,000 x 1.06^3 = 5,000 x 1.191016 = $5,955.08. Note the gain of $955.08 exceeds the $900 that simple interest would give — the extra $55.08 is [[compounding]].

questions.stem: A fund tells you it expects to distribute $10,000 to you in exactly 4 years. Using an 8% annual discount rate, what is that distribution worth today?
questions.inputHint: Answer in dollars, to the nearest cent. Do not type a $ sign.
questions.explanation: PV = 10,000 / 1.08^4. Since 1.08^4 = 1.36048896, PV = $7,350.30. Put another way, the [[discount-factor]] is 0.735 — each future dollar is worth about 74 cents today.

questions.stem: Holding the cash flow and its timing fixed, what happens to a present value when the discount rate rises?
choices: It rises, because a higher rate means a higher return
It falls, and it falls proportionally more for cash flows further in the future
It falls, by the same percentage regardless of how far away the cash flow is
It is unchanged, because the cash flow itself has not changed
rationales: This confuses the return you earn on money you hold with the value of money you are owed. A higher required return makes a fixed future promise *less* attractive to pay for today, not more.
Correct. The rate sits inside an exponent, so a larger n amplifies any change in r. This is exactly why long-duration assets fall hardest when rates rise.
The direction is right but the uniformity is wrong. Compare the discount-factor table: moving from 4% to 12% costs a 1-year dollar about 7% of its value and a 20-year dollar about 77% of its value.
The cash flow is fixed, but present value is a statement about that cash flow *and* the rate used to value it. Change either input and the answer changes.
questions.explanation: Present value moves inversely to the discount rate, and the sensitivity grows with the horizon because r compounds over n periods. This single fact drives most of what you will hear about "duration" and "rate sensitivity".

questions.stem: "Doubling the discount rate roughly halves the present value of a cash flow." True or false — and why?
justifications: False — the relationship runs through (1+r)^n, so the effect depends on the horizon and is almost never a simple halving
False — doubling the rate actually more than halves the present value in every case
True — present value is inversely proportional to the discount rate
True — but only when the cash flow is more than ten years away
rationales: Correct. There is no fixed ratio. Going from 4% to 8% on a 1-year cash flow costs about 3.7% of its value; on a 20-year cash flow it costs about 53%. The horizon decides.
Also false in its conclusion, but wrong about the reason and wrong as a universal claim — on a short-dated cash flow, doubling the rate costs far *less* than half the value.
Present value is inversely *related* to the rate, but not inversely *proportional*. Proportionality would require PV = k/r, whereas the actual relationship is PV = FV/(1+r)^n.

The horizon does control the size of the effect, but no horizon makes the halving rule reliable — at 20 years, doubling 4% to 8% cuts value by roughly half only by coincidence of those particular numbers.
questions.explanation: The trap is treating a compounding relationship as a linear one. Because r appears inside an exponent, the same change in rate produces very different proportional effects at different horizons — which is the whole reason duration exists as a concept.

questions.stem: A model discounts monthly cash flows over 5 years. The analyst has entered n = 60 and r = 0.09 (the 9% annual rate). What is the consequence?
choices: The present value will be far too low, because a 9% monthly rate is being applied 60 times
The present value will be far too high, because the rate has not been annualised
Nothing — n and r are independent inputs, so only n needs to match the cash flow frequency
The result is correct, provided the cash flows themselves are stated monthly
rationales: Correct. The model now discounts at 9% *per month* for 60 months. The divisor becomes 1.09^60, roughly 176, instead of 1.0075^60, roughly 1.57 — so present value collapses to a small fraction of the truth.
The direction is backwards. Applying too *large* a periodic rate makes the divisor too large, which makes present value too small, not too high.
They are not independent — r and n must both be expressed in the same unit of time. This is the entire point of the pitfall.
Stating the cash flows monthly fixes only one of the three inputs. The rate still has to be converted to a monthly figure.
questions.explanation: Rate and period must share a unit. For a 9% annual rate on monthly cash flows you need roughly 0.75% per month with n = 60. Saying out loud "one period is one month" before you compute is the cheapest defence against this error.

questions.stem: What is the discount factor for a cash flow arriving in 5 years, using a 7% annual discount rate?
questions.inputHint: Answer as a decimal between 0 and 1, to 3 decimal places (e.g. 0.842).
questions.explanation: The [[discount-factor]] is 1 / (1.07)^5 = 1 / 1.402552 = 0.713. Multiplying any 5-year cash flow by 0.713 converts it straight to today's dollars, which is often quicker than dividing repeatedly.

questions.stem: Four investments each promise a single payment of $1,000,000. Rates across the board rise by 2 percentage points. Which investment's present value falls by the largest percentage?
choices: The payment due in 18 months
The payment due in 5 years
The payment due in 12 years
They all fall by the same percentage, since the rate change is identical
rationales: The shortest horizon is the *least* affected. With n small, the exponent has little room to amplify the change in r.
Closer, but still not the most exposed. Five years of compounding amplifies the rate change less than twelve years does.

Correct. The longest horizon carries the largest exponent, so the same change in r compounds against it the most times. This is duration intuition: value sensitivity to rates rises with the time until the cash flow arrives.
A tempting symmetry, but wrong. The rate change is identical; its *effect* is not, because each cash flow is divided by (1+r) a different number of times.
questions.explanation: This is the seed of duration. Longer-dated cash flows are more rate-sensitive because r compounds over more periods. It is why a 30-year bond moves more than a 2-year bond on the same yield change, and why long-duration equities and long-dated private assets reprice hardest when rates move.

questions.stem: Fund A expects to return $150 million to investors in year 3. Fund B expects to return $170 million in year 7. At a 10% discount rate, which statement is correct?
choices: Fund B is worth more today, because $170 million exceeds $150 million
Fund A is worth more today, because discounting four extra years outweighs the extra $20 million
They are worth the same today, because the extra return compensates for the extra time
The comparison cannot be made without knowing each fund's management fee
rationales: This compares raw dollars while ignoring their dates — precisely the mistake the topic exists to prevent. Undiscounted totals tell you very little about relative value.
Correct. Fund A: 150 / 1.10^3 = about $112.7m. Fund B: 170 / 1.10^7 = about $87.2m. The four extra years of discounting costs far more than the extra $20 million adds.
It would take a much larger year-7 payment to draw level. At a 10% rate you would need roughly $219.6m in year 7 to match Fund A's present value.
Fees would matter for a full analysis, but the question gives you distributions and a rate, which is everything the comparison as posed requires. Refusing to answer is not the same as being rigorous.
questions.explanation: This is the everyday version of the calculation: later money needs to be *much* larger to compete with earlier money. It is also the intuition behind why returning capital early flatters an [[internal-rate-of-return]], and why the shape of a fund's cash flows matters as much as the total.
